questiontext.text: In an ISAM (Indexed Sequential Access Method) file, how are the data records physically stored?

answer.text: Sequentially, sorted by key

feedback.text: Correct — records sit in key order, which is what makes sequential and range access efficient.

answer.text: In random order, located only through a hash function

feedback.text: That describes a hash file, not ISAM.

answer.text: As a linked list with no ordering

feedback.text: ISAM keeps records physically sorted by key, not in an unordered chain.

answer.text: Scattered across overflow areas from the start

feedback.text: Overflow areas only hold later inserts; the primary records are stored sorted.

generalfeedback.text: ISAM stores records sequentially in key order so that both sequential scans and range queries are cheap.

questiontext.text: What is the job of the static index in ISAM?

answer.text: It maps key ranges to the block that contains those keys

feedback.text: Correct — the index points each key range at a data block.

answer.text: It stores every record twice for redundancy

feedback.text: The index holds key ranges and block pointers, not full duplicate records.

answer.text: It rebalances itself on every insertion

feedback.text: The ISAM index is static; it does not rebalance per insert.

answer.text: It hashes keys to random slots

feedback.text: ISAM uses an ordered index over key ranges, not hashing.

generalfeedback.text: The static index maps key ranges to blocks, letting a lookup jump near the target before scanning.

questiontext.text: How does a key lookup proceed in ISAM?

answer.text: Consult the index to find the right block, then scan that block for the key

feedback.text: Correct — the index narrows the search to one block, which is then scanned.

answer.text: Scan the whole file from the beginning every time

feedback.text: The index exists precisely to avoid a full scan.

answer.text: Compute a hash of the key and jump straight to a bucket

feedback.text: That is hashing, not the ISAM index-then-scan approach.

answer.text: Follow parent pointers up a self-balancing tree

feedback.text: ISAM uses a static index, not a dynamically balanced tree walk.

generalfeedback.text: A lookup first consults the static index to locate the block, then scans within that block for the exact key.

questiontext.text: Where do new records go when they are inserted into an ISAM file after it has been built?

answer.text: Into overflow areas, since the primary blocks are static

feedback.text: Correct — inserts land in overflow areas linked to the block.

answer.text: The index is rebuilt from scratch on every insert

feedback.text: That would be far too costly; ISAM instead uses overflow areas.

answer.text: Records are appended to the end of the file in arrival order

feedback.text: They go to overflow areas tied to the correct block, not simply the file end.

answer.text: Inserts are rejected once the file is built

feedback.text: Inserts are allowed; they are routed to overflow areas.

generalfeedback.text: Because the primary layout is static, inserts go to overflow areas, which is why performance degrades and reorganization is periodically required.

questiontext.text: Which statements about ISAM are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is well suited to range queries and sequential reads

feedback.text: Yes — sorted storage makes ranges and scans efficient.

answer.text: Heavy inserting degrades performance and calls for periodic reorganization

feedback.text: Yes — overflow chains grow, so the file is periodically reorganized.

answer.text: Its index automatically rebalances on every insertion

feedback.text: No — the ISAM index is static.

answer.text: Records are located purely by hashing with no ordering

feedback.text: No — ISAM keeps records sorted and uses an ordered index.

generalfeedback.text: ISAM excels at range/sequential access with a static index, but inserts flow to overflow areas, degrading performance until reorganization.

questiontext.text: Because records are stored in sorted key order, ISAM is well suited to range queries and sequential reads.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — sorted storage makes ranges and sequential scans efficient.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Sorted-by-key storage is exactly what makes range and sequential access cheap.

questiontext.text: ISAM never needs reorganization: no matter how many records are inserted, lookup performance stays constant.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Inserts pile into overflow areas, so performance degrades over time.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — overflow growth degrades performance, so periodic reorganization is needed.

questiontext.text: In ISAM, the static structure that maps key ranges to data blocks so a lookup can avoid a full scan is called the ______.

answer.text: index

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: index*

feedback.text: Correct.
